_comment: Unique companions (after v1): seven people who are like no one else, the same in every world; only where they are found is the world's (game/uniques.py places them). Each field: name and look (profile), who they are on the sheet (race, class, subclass, background, style, scores before race, skills, expertise, spells), the least level they join at (they come one level above the leader, or this), what they carry (kit) and the one thing that is theirs (item: a magic item with fixed properties), what they like and hate you doing (values, likes, hates, want), their gift (perk), where they are found (where, building), what the side panel and party screen say (bond, bond_text), what people say about them (rumours), their words in conversation (talk) and on the road (lines, the same kinds as data/companions.json). banter: what two of them say to each other; remembrance: Aelith on the history of a place ({text}, {year}, {place}).

osric.name: Osric Vane
osric.epithet: the last knight of the Grey Lantern
osric.title: old knight

item.title: Vigil
item.story: The sword of the Wardens of the Grey Lantern, who kept the dead in their graves for three hundred years. The light in it is older than the Order; the Order was built around it.

osric.perk_text: Keeps watch every night, whatever his orders: you are never caught asleep.
osric.speech: formal and old-fashioned, with the courtesies of a hall that no longer exists

profile.appearance: A tall old man in grey plate that has been mended with other men's armour. His beard is white and cut square; his eyes are pale and red-rimmed from nights without sleep. A lantern hangs from his belt, unlit.
profile.personality: Courteous to everyone, and tired to the bone: a man who has kept a promise so long it has become the whole of him.
profile.backstory: The last Warden of the Order of the Grey Lantern, which kept the dead in their graves. The Order was dissolved forty years ago; Osric was not told, or did not listen. He has kept the vigil over {site} alone for thirty-one years.
profile.secret: He went down into the barrow twice this winter, and came back up both times without drawing his sword. He is ashamed of it.
profile.want: for someone to finish what he cannot, so that he may put down his lantern

bond_text.default: Freed from his vigil by you, and bound to you by the only oath he has left.

rumours: They say an old knight sits by {site} every night, and has for thirty years, waiting for something inside to come out.
At {town} there is an old man in grey armour who never sleeps. He says he is a knight of an order nobody else remembers.

greet: "Evening. Or morning. I lose track." The old knight looks up from his cup, and seems to take all of you in at once.
The old knight rises when you come near, the way men were taught to rise for guests in halls that no longer stand.
ask: "A vow." He turns his cup in his hands. "I am the last Warden of the Grey Lantern. We kept the dead in their graves, once, all across these lands. The Order is forty years gone; the dead are not. {site} holds a barrow-king who will not lie still, and I have watched over him for thirty-one years." He looks at his hands. "This winter he began to walk. I went down twice. I came back up twice. I am too old, and I am ashamed, and I will not leave until it is done."
vow: Osric is quiet so long you think he has not heard. Then he stands, and bows the old way, from the waist. "Then I will wait. I am good at waiting. Bring me word that he is still, and my vigil is over."
advice: "He hates the light. Take a lantern, and keep it lit, and keep it high." Osric touches the one at his belt. "And do not let him get between you and the stair."
done: Osric goes out to {site} himself, alone, and is gone a long hour. When he comes back his face is wet and he does not hide it. "Still. After thirty-one years." He unhooks the lantern from his belt, looks at it, and hooks it back again. "Well. It seems I have a sword and nothing to guard. If you will have an old man, I am yours."
cleared: "Someone has been down into {site}." Osric looks at you, and at your boots, which are still grey with barrow-dust. "It was you. It is still, down there. I felt it go still." He stands. "Then I have a sword and nothing to guard. If you will have an old man, I am yours."
again: "Back again? Good. The barrow has been very dull with nothing in it."

hired: "The vigil is over. I find I do not know what to do with my hands."
"The Rule says a Warden goes where the dark goes. It seems the dark goes with you."
approve: "Well done. The Order would have written that down."
"Mercy is harder than the sword. You did the harder thing."
Osric inclines his head, the way knights did when there were knights.
"That was rightly done, my friend."
"I have served lords who could not have done that. Several."
disapprove: "The Rule has a word for that. I will not say it in front of you."
Osric says nothing, and his silence is as heavy as his mail.
"I have buried men who did less."
"That was beneath you. I hope."
Osric looks at you the way he looks at a barrow at dusk: waiting to see what comes out.
complain: "I kept a vigil thirty-one years. I can keep my patience a little longer. Not much longer."
Osric polishes Vigil in silence all evening, and does not look at you.
"The Order taught me to follow. It did not teach me to follow just anyone."
desert: Osric is gone in the morning. He has banked the fire, and left a note in a careful old hand: "The Rule forbids me this company. Forgive me."
leave: "I will go back to my barrow. Somebody should watch it, even empty. Send for me if you need a sword."
Osric bows, the old way, and walks off with his lantern swinging at his belt.
devoted: "I swore my oath to the Order once. It is gone. I will swear it to you, if you will have it."
Osric has started to sleep a little, when you are the one on watch. He says it is the first rest he has had in thirty years.
battle: "Stand fast! The Lantern stands!"
Osric raises Vigil, and its light goes hard and white.
"Behind me. All of you."
"For the Grey Lantern!" The cry has not been heard in forty years; Osric makes up for it.
"Come, then. I have waited long enough."
camp: Osric does not sleep. He sits with Vigil across his knees and watches the dark until dawn, and says he has slept enough for one life.
Osric recites the Rule of the Lantern, all forty-one articles, and apologises for the forty-second, which he has forgotten.
Osric oils his armour by the fire, plate by plate, the way another man might say his prayers.
Osric tells you about the chapter-house of the Order: its long table, its bell, its forty knights. He is the only one left who remembers the bell.
"The dead are quiet tonight," Osric says, the way another man might say it was cold.
level_up: "An old dog, and a new trick. Who knew."
Osric moves easier in his harness than he did. "Use," he says. "The armour remembers."
mood_good: "Better than I have been in forty years. There is something to keep watch over again."
mood_fair: "I am old, and the road is long. Otherwise, well enough."
"I have known better nights, and a great many worse."
mood_bad: "I have been thinking about my barrow. That is never a good sign."
"Do not ask me that, and I will not have to tell you."
road: Osric: "This road ran to a chapter-house once. There is nothing there now but nettles."
Osric walks with his hand on his sword hilt, the way old soldiers do, as if to be sure it is still there.
Osric: "Forty years since the Order fell. You would think I would have stopped counting."
Osric stops at a wayside grave to straighten its stone, and catches up without a word.
Osric: "A Warden walks at the back. That is where the dead come from."
Osric hums a hymn of the Order, very low, and loses the tune in the same place every time.
road_tired: Osric is breathing hard, and pretends he is not. "Old," he says. "Not dead."
Osric: "When I was young I walked this in a day. In armour. Uphill."
road_wet: Osric's armour rusts as you watch. He oils it at every halt, grimly.
Osric: "Rain in the joints. Mine and the armour's."
road_night: Osric draws Vigil a hand's breadth from its sheath, and a pale light comes out to walk with you.
Osric: "Night is when I am at work. Walk behind me."
Osric lifts his head at a sound in the dark, listens, and walks on. "Only the living," he says.
road_cold: Osric: "Cold is nothing. I have spent thirty winters on a barrow."
Frost silvers Osric's beard. He does not seem to notice.
road_hot: Osric bakes in his plate and will not take it off. "The dead do not wait for cool weather."

durgin.name: Durgin Ashbeard
durgin.epithet: last of the clan of Kharak-Dûl
durgin.title: old dwarf

item.title: Ashguard
item.story: The door of the forge-hall of Kharak-Dûl, cut down to a shield. It was the only thing in the hold the wyrm could not melt, and Durgin has carried it ever since.

durgin.perk_text: Knows where every dragon in the land sleeps, and carries a shield no fire can get through.
durgin.speech: short and gruff, in a deep voice, with the odd dwarvish oath

profile.appearance: A dwarf with a beard the grey of cold ash, worn in two plaits and tucked into his belt. His left hand is a knot of old burn-scar. He sits with his back to the wall, and beside him leans a shield that has been in a fire and does not seem to have minded.
profile.personality: Gruff, patient as stone, and funny in a way that takes a while to notice. Keeps a small black book of every wrong ever done to him, and reads from it.
profile.backstory: Durgin was forty, a boy by dwarven reckoning, when {dragon} came down on Kharak-Dûl and burned it hall by hall. He got out through the drains with his grandfather's shield. He has spent a hundred and seventy years learning how dragons live, and how they die.
profile.secret: He has been to the mouth of {site} three times, and three times turned back at the smell. He does not know whether he is a coward. He means to find out.
profile.want: to put {dragon} in the ground, and then to go home, though there is no home

bond_text.default: Sworn with you against {dragon}. Stone hear it, ash remember it.
bond_text.avenged: Avenged at last, and staying because you are the nearest thing to a clan he has.
bond_text.free: Has nothing left to do but fight, and has chosen to do it beside you.

rumours: There's a dwarf drinking himself to death at {town}. They say he knows where {dragon} sleeps, and means to kill it, and has meant to for a hundred years.
An old dwarf at {town} will drink with anyone who asks, and tell them about a burned hold, if they are still sitting up by the end.

greet: "If you're not buying, you're not sitting." The dwarf does not look up from his mug.
The old dwarf looks you up and down, slowly, and writes something in a small black book.
win: You match him mug for mug, and then one more. Durgin sets his down, wipes his beard, and looks at you properly for the first time. "Stone and ash. You'll do. Sit." And he tells you about Kharak-Dûl, and the wyrm {dragon}, and the hundred and seventy years since.
lose: Somewhere around the ninth mug the room begins to turn. You wake with your face on the table and Durgin gone. He laughed, the innkeeper says, and left word: "Come back tomorrow. If you can walk."
unblooded: "Swear? With you?" Durgin laughs into his beer. "You'd be ash before you saw its teeth. Come back when you've killed something bigger than a rat."
oath: Durgin spits in his palm and holds it out. "Then it's sworn. Stone hear it, ash remember it." His grip is like a closing door. "{dragon} sleeps under {site}. I'll show you the way. I've walked it in my head every night for a hundred years."
no_dragon: "Someone else killed it." Durgin stares at his mug. "A hundred and seventy years, and someone else." He is quiet a long while. "Well. I've nothing left to do but fight. You look like you could use that."
avenged: Durgin kneels by what is left of {dragon} and says something in the old tongue that takes a long time. When he stands, he takes out his black book, finds a page near the front, and draws a line through it. "There," he says. "Done." And then, to everyone's surprise, he laughs until he cries.
oathbreak: "You swore." Durgin does not raise his voice; that is the worst of it. "Stone heard you." He writes your name in the book, on the other page, and walks away without looking back.
again: "Back? Good. The beer here is a disgrace and I've read my book twice."

hired: "Right. Where's my beer. No? Right. Onward, then."
Durgin shoulders his shield. "Stone hear it."
approve: "Hah! That goes in the Book, on the good page."
"Not bad, for somebody who'll be dead in forty years."
Durgin grunts, which from him is a speech.
"My grandfather would have bought you a drink for that. Then fought you for it."
disapprove: "That goes in the Book. The other page."
Durgin takes out a small black book, licks a stub of pencil, and writes something down without a word.
"Dwarves remember. Just so you know."
"Humans. You'd sell your own mothers for a dry bed."
complain: Durgin reads from his Book of Grudges by the fire, loudly, and your name comes up more than once.
"I've waited a hundred and seventy years. I'm starting to think I'll be waiting longer with you."
"If I wanted to walk in circles I'd have stayed at the alehouse."
desert: Durgin is gone by morning, and the last page of his book has your name on it, underlined twice.
leave: "Right. I'll be at the alehouse. Same stool. Probably the same beer."
Durgin nods once, stiffly, and goes, and does not look back, which is how dwarves say goodbye.
devoted: "I've carried the Book alone a hundred and seventy years. You can hold it a while, if you like. Mind the pages."
Durgin has started calling you 'clan' when he thinks you can't hear.
battle: "Ash and stone!"
"KHARAK-DÛL!"
Durgin laughs, a sound like rocks going down a well, and wades in.
"Get behind the shield! What do you think it's for?"
"Is that all? I've fought worse in my sleep. I've fought worse IN my sleep."
camp: Durgin reads from his Book of Grudges by the fire. It is very long. You are in it, he says, but only in pencil.
Durgin carves a little stone dragon by the firelight, and then breaks it in half, and then carves another.
Durgin tells you how Kharak-Dûl looked from the valley at sunset, with every window lit. He tells it the same way every time.
Durgin sleeps sitting up, with his back to a rock and his shield across his knees.
"Humans cook everything too fast," Durgin says, and takes over.
level_up: "Two hundred years old and still learning. My father would be sick."
Durgin tries a new swing, and nods at it. "Aye. That'll do for a dragon."
mood_good: "Good. Good as a dwarf gets, anyhow, outside a mountain."
mood_fair: "I've been worse, and I'll be worse again."
mood_bad: "Ask me again after I've killed something."
road: Durgin: "Hills. Hills are just mountains that gave up."
Durgin counts the days since Kharak-Dûl burned. It is a large number and he says all of it.
Durgin looks at the sky, sniffs, and says it will rain in three hours. It does.
Durgin: "Humans build walls out of wood. Wood. And then they're surprised."
Durgin stops to look at a cut in a hillside, and says the rock is good and the people who quarried it were fools.
road_tired: Durgin: "I'm not tired. Dwarves don't get tired. We get... thoughtful."
Durgin walks slower, but no one could say he walks lighter.
road_wet: Durgin wrings out his beard, both plaits, and says a word in Dwarvish that makes the rain seem to stop and listen.
Durgin: "Under a mountain it never rains. I'm just saying."
road_night: Durgin: "Dark's nothing. Try being under a mountain when the lamps go out."
Durgin can see in the dark, and tells you about everything he can see, which does not help.
road_cold: Durgin: "Cold? This isn't cold. The gatehouse of Kharak-Dûl in winter, that was cold."
road_hot: Durgin: "This is nothing. You should feel a dragon breathe."
Durgin sweats, and grumbles, and will not take off a single ring of his mail.

tobiah.name: Tobiah Vell
tobiah.epithet: the thief the rope will not take
tobiah.title: prisoner

item.title: The Hangman's Knot
item.story: The knot from the second rope, the one that slipped. He cut it off the gallows himself that night, and has worn it round his neck ever since, for luck. It seems to work.

tobiah.perk_text: Cannot be killed the first time each day: a blow that should drop him leaves him standing.
tobiah.speech: quick and cheerful, never stops talking, full of gutter slang and bad jokes

profile.appearance: A thin, quick man with a rope-scar round his throat like a collar, and another, fainter, just above it. He has the easy grin of somebody who has already had the worst day of his life, twice, and found both of them survivable.
profile.personality: Cheerful, talkative, light-fingered, and loyal to a fault to anyone who does him a good turn. Cannot pass a purse without weighing it, and usually gives it back.
profile.backstory: A thief from the gutters of {town}, hanged for stealing a bishop's ring. The rope broke. He was hanged again a month later; the hangman had been paid in false coin, and tied a knot to match. The law says a man the rope refuses three times is pardoned by the gods, so {town} has kept him in its cells for a year rather than find out.
profile.secret: He did steal the ring. He gave it to a woman who needed it more than the bishop did, and he would do it again.
profile.want: out, and then somebody worth being loyal to

bond_text.default: Owes you his neck, and means to pay it back with interest.

rumours: They have a thief in the cells at {town} who has been hanged twice and lived. The whole town is betting on the third rope.
Tobiah Vell, the one they call Twice-Hanged, is still in {town}'s cells. Nobody dares to hang him again.

greet: "If you've come to see the man who can't be hanged, it's a copper to look and two to ask questions. I'm joking. Mostly."
hello: Tobiah leans on the bars as if they were a tavern counter. "There are three ways out of here: the gaoler's purse, the gaoler's good opinion, and the gaoler's lock. I'm not proud. Any of them will do."
paid: The gaoler counts your coin twice and opens the door. Tobiah steps out, stretches, and somehow, on the way past the gaoler's table, recovers his boots, his knife, his picks and, you suspect, the gaoler's lunch. "I owe you my neck," he says. "It's a good neck. Third-hand, but good."
spoke: You talk; the gaoler listens; somewhere in the middle he starts to laugh. "Take him. The whole town's been betting on the third rope and I've lost money twice." Tobiah is out, and has his boots back, before the key has stopped turning.
spoke_no: The gaoler hears you out and shakes his head. "He's worth more to the town where he is. The betting alone." Tobiah, behind the bars, shrugs cheerfully. "Worth a try. Come back tomorrow. I'll be here."
picked: It is a bad lock and a worse gaoler. Tobiah is out and down the passage before the tumblers have stopped clicking, and he waits for you round the corner, grinning. "Now THAT," he says, "is how you do it."
picked_no: The lock is better than it looks. You hear boots on the stair and step away just in time. Tobiah winks. "Tomorrow. Bring a smaller pick."
again: "You again! I knew you'd miss me. Everyone does, eventually."

hired: "Right! Where are we going? No, don't tell me. Surprise me."
approve: "Oh, that was lovely. That was art."
"I like you more every day. It's alarming."
Tobiah whistles, low and impressed.
"Now that's how you treat people. Somebody should write it down. Not me, I can't spell."
disapprove: "I've been on the wrong end of that. Twice. It's worse than it looks."
Tobiah stops smiling, which is the only time you have ever seen him do it.
"You know, I've met hangmen with more heart."
"Don't. Just... don't do that again."
complain: "You know what the cells had that this doesn't? A roof. And the company was better."
Tobiah steals your spoon, and does not give it back, which he always used to.
desert: Tobiah is gone in the morning, and so, you find, is a good deal of your coin. He has left a note: "Sorry. Old habits."
leave: "Well! It's been lovely. If you ever need anything stolen, you know where the gaol is."
Tobiah shakes your hand, and when he has gone you check your purse. It's all there. You feel oddly touched.
devoted: "Here. It's your purse. I took it the first day, just to see. I've been carrying it back ever since, waiting for the right moment."
"You know, I'd hang for you. Third time. I mean it."
battle: "Oh, this'll be fun. For one of us."
"I've been hanged twice, lads. You don't scare me."
Tobiah vanishes from where he was and turns up somewhere worse for them.
"Mind the knees! Everyone forgets the knees!"
camp: Tobiah juggles three knives and an apple by the fire, and eats the apple.
Tobiah tells the story of his first hanging. It is very funny, somehow, until the end.
Tobiah picks every lock in the party's packs, to keep in practice, and locks them all again.
Tobiah sleeps with one hand on his throat, and says it's just a habit.
level_up: "Getting good, aren't I? Don't answer that."
Tobiah's hands are quicker than they were, and he knows it, and shows everybody.
mood_good: "Never better! Well. Never better with a rope scar."
"Honestly? I'm having the time of my life. It's been a short life, but still."
mood_bad: "You want the truth? I'm thinking about the rope again."
"Ask me tomorrow. Tomorrow's always better. That's the whole trick."
road: Tobiah: "You can tell a rich man's house by the doorstep. Worn in the middle, poor. Worn at the edges, rich. The servants walk at the edges."
Tobiah walks backwards for a mile, talking, and never once trips.
Tobiah: "Third time's the charm, they say. I'd rather not find out."
Tobiah tries to teach someone to pick a pocket, using your pocket.
Tobiah waves at a man in a field, who waves back, and then checks his purse.
road_tired: Tobiah: "My feet are telling me things I don't want to hear."
Tobiah stops talking, which tells you how tired he is.
road_wet: Tobiah: "The cells were dry. I'm just saying. Dry, and they brought soup."
Tobiah puts his hood up and his hands in somebody else's pockets.
road_night: Tobiah is in his element in the dark, and becomes very hard to see.
Tobiah: "This is the good time. The honest folk are all asleep."
road_cold: Tobiah: "Cold enough to freeze a rope stiff. Which, now I think of it..."
road_hot: Tobiah: "Hot enough to hang a man. They like to do it in summer, you know. Draws a crowd."

wendeline.name: Wendeline Rook
wendeline.title: plague-nurse

item.title: The Plague-Bell
item.story: A hand-bell of dull bronze on a cord round her neck, rung ahead of her on the plague roads so the sick know someone is coming. It has rung over four thousand graves, and it has a way of mending what it rings over.

wendeline.perk_text: Has never caught a sickness and never will; her bell heals, and her hands know every wound.
wendeline.speech: blunt and dry, like a tired ward-sister, with a gravedigger's jokes

profile.appearance: A broad, weathered woman in a grey habit gone brown at the hem, a bronze bell on a cord round her neck, and a shovel over her shoulder that has seen more use than the bell. Her hands are red from lye and very clean.
profile.personality: Blunt, tired, and funnier than a nun has any right to be. She has buried too many people to be frightened of anything, and too many children to be patient with fools.
profile.backstory: Sister Wendeline left her convent twenty years ago to walk wherever the plague was, ringing a bell so the sick would know somebody was coming. She has buried, by her own count, four thousand four hundred and eleven people. She has never once been ill.
profile.secret: She stopped believing in God during the great sickness eleven years ago, and has not told anyone, and has not stopped praying.
profile.want: to be somewhere the bell is needed

bond_text.default: Walks with you because the bell is needed wherever you are going.

rumours: There's a nun with a bell who walks wherever the sickness is. They say she has buried four thousand and never once caught it. She is at {town} now.
The bell-woman is at {town}, they say, tending the sick nobody else will go near.

greet: Wendeline does not stop working. "If you're sick, lie down over there. If you're not, you can carry water."
"Wash your hands before you come any closer." The nun does not look round.
worked: You carry water and lift the dying and dig, and by evening you no longer notice the smell. Wendeline watches you work. At the end of the day she rings her bell once, for the ones you lost, and says: "You've done this before. Or you learn quick."
worked_no: You are more hindrance than help, and she tells you so, not unkindly. "Go and wash. Come back tomorrow, if you mean it."
come: Wendeline looks round at the beds, and at the graves outside, and nods slowly. "The worst is over here. There's always somewhere worse." She picks up her bell and her shovel. "I'll walk with you. The bell's needed on the road too."
heard: "You're the one who brought the medicine to {cured}." Wendeline looks you up and down. "Well. Somebody has to walk with the ones who do that."
not_yet: "I can't leave them. Not while there's work." She nods at the beds. "Help, if you want to help."
infamous: "I know what they say about you." She does not stop working. "I've buried enough of your sort's work."
again: "Back, are you? Good. Nobody here's dying fast enough to need me."

hired: "Right. Show me who's hurt. There's always someone."
Wendeline rings her bell once, for the road.
approve: "That was kind. Don't let it go to your head."
"Good. That's one grave fewer."
Wendeline nods, once, and goes back to what she was doing, which from her is praise.
"The world's a little less heavy for that. Only a little. It adds up."
disapprove: "I'll be the one who buries that. I always am."
"Four thousand, four hundred and twelve. Don't make it thirteen."
Wendeline says nothing. She rings her bell once, for whoever it was.
"God forgives you. I'm not God, and I'll take my time."
complain: "There are sick people everywhere, and we are walking straight past them."
Wendeline goes to bed early and does not say goodnight.
desert: Wendeline is gone in the morning. She has left the herbs and bandages sorted and labelled, and a note: "There's plague in the east. You'll manage."
leave: "Well. There's always somewhere the bell's needed." And she goes, ringing it.
Wendeline squeezes your hand hard enough to hurt. "Wash your wounds. Properly."
devoted: "I stopped counting the dead a few weeks ago. I only just noticed. That's your doing."
"Whatever comes, I'll be the one who carries you out. Remember that."
battle: "Mind yourselves! I'm not sewing anyone up twice today!"
Wendeline hitches up her habit and wades in with her staff.
"God and the bell! And the staff! Mostly the staff!"
"Try not to die. It makes so much work."
camp: Wendeline looks at everyone's wounds before her own, and scolds everyone about them.
Wendeline tells you about the worst plague she ever walked through. She tells it plainly, and nobody sleeps well.
Wendeline scrubs her hands until they are red, and then scrubs yours.
Wendeline prays, briefly and without much hope, and then sleeps like a stone.
"Four thousand, four hundred and eleven," Wendeline tells the fire. "I count them. Somebody should."
level_up: Wendeline flexes her fingers. "The Lord gives, now and then."
mood_good: "Nobody's died this week. I don't know what to do with myself."
"Well enough. Better than the people I usually walk with."
mood_fair: "Tired. I'm always tired. It's the job."
"Alive, and so are you. Let's not complain."
mood_bad: "I've buried better than you, and worse. The worse ones were heavier."
"Don't. I'm not in the mood for kindness."
road: Wendeline: "Wash your hands. No, properly."
Wendeline rings the bell as you pass a lone grave by the road, and does not explain.
Wendeline names every plant by the road, and what it cures, and what it kills.
Wendeline: "I walked this road in the sickness year. Every house had a cross on the door. Look at it now."
Wendeline stops to look at a child's cut knee at a farm gate, and catches up ten minutes later.
road_tired: Wendeline: "I've walked further on worse feet. Keep going."
road_night: Wendeline rings the bell softly in the dark, and the dark seems to make room for it.
Wendeline: "The sick always get worse at night. Walk quicker."
road_cold: Wendeline: "Keep your feet dry. Frostbite takes toes, and I'm not taking them off for you."
road_hot: Wendeline: "Drink. Drink before you're thirsty. Nobody ever listens."

grusha.name: Grusha Nine-Fingers
grusha.title: penitent

item.title: Penance
item.story: A smith's maul from the temple forge. She has broken down a great many doors with it since, and every one of them, she says, was to let somebody out.

grusha.perk_text: Orcs and goblins know her name: with her beside you, they will often let you talk your way past.
grusha.speech: very few words, short and plain, never a word more than she needs

profile.appearance: A big half-orc woman in a temple servant's smock, her tusks filed blunt, scrubbing the floor with a brush in each hand. Her left hand has four fingers and a smooth stump. She does not look up.
profile.personality: Says little, and all of it true. Does the hardest and dirtiest work there is without being asked. Under the quiet there is still the raider she was, and she keeps it on a very short chain.
profile.backstory: At nineteen Grusha rode with the Red Hand, and helped to burn {village}. She stopped halfway through, with an axe raised over a child, and has never understood why. The band left her for dead; a priest's widow in the ruins of {village} nursed her. She cut off her own finger the day she put down the axe, and has scrubbed temple floors for twenty years.
profile.secret: The child she did not kill is grown now, and lives in {village}, and she knows the name.
profile.want: to go back to {village}, and say what she did, and take what comes

bond_text.default: Walking with you to {village}, to answer for what she did there.
bond_text.forgiven: Forgiven at {village}, and yours for as long as you want her.
bond_text.paid: Paid for at {village}, if not forgiven. She says that is fair.
bond_text.unforgiven: Unforgiven at {village}. She carries it, and follows you.

rumours: There's an orc woman scrubbing the temple floors at {town}. Twenty years, they say. Nobody knows what she's paying for.
The penitent at {town}'s temple was a raider once. They say she burned a village, and cut off her own finger for it.

greet: The half-orc keeps scrubbing, and does not look up.
"Mind the wet." She moves her bucket out of your way without raising her eyes.
tell: Grusha keeps scrubbing. "I rode with the Red Hand. Nineteen winters old. We burned {village}." The brush stops. "I had the axe up over a child, and I did not bring it down. I do not know why. They left me for dead. A widow there nursed me." She holds up her hand: four fingers and the stump. "I took that myself, the day I put the axe down. Twenty years I have scrubbed floors. I want to go back. I want to tell them what I did, and take what comes." She goes back to scrubbing. "An orc alone on the road is hanged at the first tree."
hiding: "Floors are safe," Grusha says. "Floors do not look at you." It is a long time before she says anything else.
ready: Grusha stops. For a long moment she looks at the brush in her hand as if she has never seen it before. "You are right," she says. "I have been hiding. Twenty years."
go: Grusha puts down the brushes, both of them, very carefully, side by side. Then she stands, and she is much bigger standing. "I will carry your packs," she says. "I will do the fighting you do not want to do. And at {village} I will answer."
infamous: Grusha looks at you once. "No. I have ridden with your kind. I will not do it again."
arrive: The people of {village} know Grusha. Faces go still; a child is called indoors. Word runs ahead of you, and by the time you reach the well, {headman} is waiting, with half the village behind.
forgiven: A woman at the back of the crowd pushes to the front. "I was the child," she says. "The one you did not kill." Grusha kneels in the mud. The woman puts a hand on her head, and leaves it there. When Grusha stands she is weeping, and does not hide it, and neither does anyone else.
unforgiven: "No." {headman} does not raise their voice. "Not today. Maybe not ever. Take her away from here." Grusha bows, and turns, and walks out of {village} with her back very straight.
paid: The blood-price is counted into {headman}'s hands, coin by coin, in silence. "It does not bring them back," {headman} says. "But it will rebuild the mill. Go."
hanged: Grusha walks to the tree herself. She does not look back. {village} has waited twenty years, and does not hurry now.
walked: You take Grusha away before anything can be decided. The stones start when you reach the gate. Grusha shields you from them with her own back, and says nothing for the rest of the day.
again: Grusha puts down her brush. She does not ask where. She never does.

hired: Grusha picks up the heaviest pack without being asked.
"Good. Walk. I will be behind you."
approve: "Good." From Grusha, that is a great deal.
Grusha nods, slowly, as if she were putting it somewhere safe.
"That is what I would do now. Not what I would have done then."
disapprove: "I did that, once. Look where it got me."
Grusha's hands close into fists, and then, slowly, open.
"No. That is the Red Hand's way. Not ours."
Grusha looks at her missing finger for a long time.
complain: Grusha works in silence all day, and in silence is not the same as quiet.
"I left the floors for this. Remind me why."
desert: Grusha is gone in the morning. Everything she carried has been set down neatly by the fire, sorted, with nothing missing.
leave: Grusha nods, and goes back the way she came, towards her floors.
"If you need something heavy carried, or somebody hit, you know where I scrub."
devoted: "I have a clan again. It is a strange clan. I will keep it."
Grusha has started to hum as she walks: an orcish marching song, with the words changed.
battle: Grusha roars, and for a moment she is nineteen again, and terrible.
"Come on, then!"
"Stand aside. I know how they think. I thought it."
Grusha says a prayer, very fast, and then swings Penance with both hands.
camp: Grusha scrubs the cooking pot until it shines, then scrubs it again.
Grusha tells you, in very few words, what the Red Hand did at the fords. Then she goes to sleep, and you do not.
Grusha prays at the edge of the firelight, kneeling in the cold, for a long time.
Grusha sharpens nothing, mends everything, and says nothing.
level_up: Grusha swings Penance, and the air seems to get out of its way.
mood_good: "Good. I am... good." She seems surprised by it.
"The road is better than the floors. Do not tell the priest."
mood_fair: "I have been worse. I have been much worse."
mood_bad: Grusha just looks at her hand.
road: Grusha walks at the back, where she can see everyone.
Grusha: "The Red Hand came this way once. Or a road like it."
Grusha steps off the road to let a farmer's cart go by, head down, the way she has learned to.
A child at a gate stares at Grusha's tusks. Grusha bares them, very gently, and the child laughs.
road_tired: Grusha carries someone's pack as well as her own, and does not mention it.
road_wet: Grusha lifts her face to the rain, and seems to like it.
road_night: Grusha sees in the dark, and walks ahead now, quiet as a cat.
road_cold: Grusha: "Cold is good. Cold keeps you awake."
road_hot: Grusha sweats, and says nothing, and carries more.

aelith.name: Aelith Oriel
aelith.title: keeper of the memory-books

item.title: The Last Leaf
item.story: A ring of pale wood that has not grown in seven hundred years. It was cut from the last tree of a wood that is now the bottom of a lake.

aelith.perk_text: Remembers the history of every place you walk into, and knows every magic thing at a glance.
aelith.speech: precise, cool and old-fashioned; corrects people, and remembers everything

profile.appearance: An elf who looks forty and holds herself as if she were four hundred, which is a lie in the other direction. Ink on her fingers, a ring of pale wood, and grey eyes that look at you the way a scholar looks at a page: reading.
profile.personality: Precise, dry, and impatient with everything short-lived, which is everything. Sad underneath it, and very well hidden.
profile.backstory: Aelith has kept the memory-books of her people for five hundred years: every king, every war, every burned town in these lands, written down while it happened. She has decided that this age is ending, and that she would rather see the end of it than read about it afterwards.
profile.secret: She has already written the end of the book, in a sealed quire at the back. She wants to know whether she was right.
profile.want: to be told something she does not already know

bond_text.default: Came to see how this age ends, and is writing it down as it goes.

rumours: At {town} there is an elf who has written down everything that ever happened. They say she will follow anyone who can tell her something she doesn't know.
The Remembrancer of {town} is looking for news, they say. Real news: the kind nobody has written down yet.

greet: "You are standing in my light." The elf does not look up from her page.
"Another visitor." She marks her place with one long finger. "Speak, then. Briefly."
ask: "Something I do not know." Aelith does not look up. "I have written down everything that has happened in these lands for five hundred years. Tell me one thing I have not written, and I will come with you and see how this age ends. I have decided that it is ending."
book: Aelith takes the book and reads it where she stands, a page a breath, and hands it back. "The dates are wrong, the author was a fool, and I did not know about the ford at the end." She sounds almost pleased. "Very well. I will come, and see how it ends."
told: You tell her about a place you have been. She stops you twice to correct you, and once, only once, she writes something down. "I did not know that," she says. Then, quietly, as if it costs her something: "Very well. I will come with you, and see how this ends."
told_no: "Yes. I know. I was there." Aelith turns back to her books. "Tell me something I do not know."
shown: Aelith takes it from you and turns it over in her long fingers. "{item}. Of course." She tells you exactly what it is, and hands it back. "Where did you find it?" You tell her. "Then you go to interesting places. I will come."
again: "You again. Good. The age did not end while you were away. I checked."

hired: Aelith closes her book, marks the page, and follows you out as if she has done it a thousand times. She may have.
approve: "Well done. I shall write that down."
"Hm. That was not what I expected. Good."
Aelith raises one eyebrow, which from her is applause.
"There. That is the kind of thing that gets remembered."
disapprove: "I have written that down too. In a different ink."
"Every age has its fools. I did hope you would not be this one's."
Aelith looks at you as if you were a mistake in the margin.
"How very human of you."
complain: "I have outlived three kingdoms and a language. I can outlive this. Probably."
Aelith reads all evening and does not answer when she is spoken to.
desert: Aelith is gone in the morning. She has left a page, neatly written, describing you. It is not kind, and it is entirely accurate.
leave: "I have enough for a chapter." Aelith closes her book. "Not a long one."
Aelith nods, and goes back to her books, and you have the feeling you are already being written down.
devoted: "I have decided to put you in the book. The real book. Very few people are in the real book."
"You are the most interesting thing to happen in two hundred years. Do not let it go to your head."
battle: "How tedious." Aelith's hands move, and the air goes cold.
"Stand back. I have done this before, and I am better at it than you."
Aelith speaks a word that has not been spoken aloud in three hundred years.
"Try not to bleed on my books."
camp: Aelith writes by the firelight, very small and very neat, and will not say what.
Aelith explains the stars to anyone who will listen. She knew some of them when they were brighter.
Aelith corrects the story someone is telling at the fire. Then she tells it properly, and it is better.
Aelith does not sleep; elves do not. She sits very still with her eyes open, remembering.
"In my first century," Aelith begins, and everyone settles in.
level_up: "I remember this. It comes back, a little at a time."
Aelith turns a page of her spellbook that she has not turned in a hundred years.
mood_good: "Content. It is a rare thing at my age. Do not spoil it."
"This is the most I have enjoyed a century in some time."
mood_fair: "Well enough. Everything is well enough, when you have seen what I have."
mood_bad: "I am considering going home. I have been considering it for some days."
"Do you know how many people like you I have outlived?"
road: Aelith: "This was forest once. All of it. I walked here when I was young."
Aelith names every hill you pass, with the names they had four hundred years ago.
Aelith: "Humans. You burn so brightly and so briefly. Like moths. Clever moths, some of you."
Aelith stops to read an old stone by the road, and laughs once, sharply, at something on it.
Aelith walks as if the road were a library and she were looking for one particular book.
road_tired: Aelith is not tired. She says so. She says so again, a mile later.
road_wet: Aelith walks through the rain as if it were falling on somebody else.
Aelith: "It rained like this the year the old king died. It rains like this every year, in fact."
road_night: Aelith sees perfectly in the dark, and walks in front, and does not slow down for anybody.
Aelith: "The stars have moved since I was young. Not much. Enough."
road_cold: Aelith: "This is not cold. The winter of the long night, that was cold. You would not remember it."
road_hot: Aelith: "The summer the river dried was hotter than this. That was three hundred and eleven years ago."

wren.name: Wren Underbough
wren.title: halfling carter

item.title: The Coat of Many Pockets
item.story: Forty-one pockets, by her count, and eleven of them the wardens of every walled town in the land have never found. She sewed the last one herself, in a gaol cell, and walked out wearing it.

wren.perk_text: Gate-wardens never search your packs while she is with you, and nobody gets lost with her.
wren.speech: brisk and merry, calls everyone 'love', full of road-lore and smugglers' cant

profile.appearance: A halfling in a long oilskin coat with far too many pockets, a pipe she never lights, and the weathered look of somebody who sleeps under carts. Everything about her is either strapped down or hidden.
profile.personality: Brisk, merry, practical, and never in a hurry, which is how she has never been caught. Loves food, hates bullies, and has an opinion about every road in the land.
profile.backstory: Wren has run cargo along the back roads for thirty years: salt past the king's tax, books past the priests, people past the watch. She knows every gate-warden in every walled town by name, and what each of them likes to drink. She has never been caught, and she is starting to get bored.
profile.secret: The last cargo she ran was a family of heretics, who were taken at the border because she was late. She has not been late since, and she has not run anything since either.
profile.want: one last good run, with somebody who has the nerve for it

bond_text.default: Came along for one last good run, and has not found it yet.

rumours: They say the best smuggler on the back roads is a halfling woman at {town}, and she has never once been caught.
Want something carried past a gate? Ask for Wren at {town}. Ask quietly.

greet: "Evening, love. You look like you've come a long way by the wrong roads."
The halfling tips her hat without taking the unlit pipe out of her mouth. "Buying, selling, or lost?"
cargo: Wren looks you over the way a horse-trader looks at a horse. "I've a crate," she says. "It wants to go to {recipient} in {dest}, and it doesn't want the wardens at the gate looking in it. Get it there, and I'll know you've got the nerve. Then we'll talk."
waiting: "Still got my crate? Good. Don't open it. Really, love, don't."
done: "Delivered? Past the gate? And nobody looked?" Wren grins, and knocks out her unlit pipe. "You'll do. I've been wanting to see what's over the mountains before I'm too old to climb them. Let's go."
guild: Wren looks at your hands, and makes a small sign with hers, and you make the answering one. "Well, then. Any friend of the Guild." She is already packing. "I was getting bored anyway."
gate: Wren talks to the wardens about the weather, their mothers and the price of salt. They wave you through without looking at anything.
"Evening, Hob," Wren says to the gate-warden, who grins and waves you all through. "Old friend," she says afterwards. "Owes me for his daughter's wedding."
The wardens start towards your packs; Wren says a name, very quietly; they stop, and find something else to look at.
again: "Knew you'd be back. They always come back. It's the pockets."

hired: "Right. Rule one: we never take the king's road when there's a sheep-track going the same way."
Wren checks forty-one pockets in turn, and nods. "Ready."
approve: "Oh, nicely done."
"Now that's what I call a clean job."
Wren grins round her pipe.
"You're wasted on honest work, you know."
disapprove: "That's the kind of thing that gets people hanged. Usually the wrong people."
"No. Bullying's bullying, whoever does it."
Wren takes her pipe out of her mouth, which she only does when she means it.
"I've left partners at the side of the road for less."
complain: "This is a slow run, and I don't like slow runs."
Wren is quiet for a whole day, which is unheard of.
desert: Wren is gone in the morning, and so is the best of the food. A note says: "Sorry, love. Old habits. Don't look for me; you won't find me. Nobody ever has."
leave: "Well, it's been a run. Not the best run. Not the worst either." And she's gone down a lane you hadn't noticed.
Wren tips her hat. "If you ever need something moved, you know how to ask. Quietly."
devoted: "Thirty years on the back roads and I never had a partner I trusted. Funny, isn't it."
"I'd run anything for you. Anything. Even honest goods."
battle: "Why is it always swords with you people?"
Wren disappears into the nearest shadow and comes out of a different one.
"Right, right, right. Stay calm. Hit them in the soft bits."
"Not the pockets! Not the pockets!"
camp: Wren cooks. Everybody lets her. It is the best thing that happens all day.
Wren tells you the story of the three bishops and the barrel of eels, and will not say which parts are true.
Wren sews a new pocket into her coat. "Forty-two," she says.
"Second supper," Wren announces, and nobody argues.
Wren teaches someone the smugglers' cant. The word for 'gate-warden' is very rude.
level_up: "Still learning. That's the secret. Never stop learning, never get caught."
Wren's hands are quicker than they were. She notices before anybody else does.
mood_good: "Lovely day for it. Whatever it is."
"I've had worse partners. I've had much worse partners."
mood_fair: "Fair to middling. Like the ale round here."
"Could be better. Could always be better."
mood_bad: "Honestly? I'm thinking about the back roads. On my own."
road: Wren: "Never take the king's road when there's a sheep-track going the same way."
Wren takes you by a path you would never have seen, and it saves an hour.
Wren: "See that inn? Don't eat the pie. Don't ever eat the pie."
Wren knows the name of every farm dog you pass, and most of them know hers.
Wren: "Second breakfast is a state of mind."
Wren points out a hollow tree where she once hid a bishop's silver for a year.
road_tired: Wren: "My feet have walked a hundred thousand miles. They've earned a rest. They're not getting one, but they've earned it."
road_wet: Wren's coat sheds the rain like a duck. Nobody else's does, and she is smug about it.
road_night: Wren: "Night's for working. Day's for looking innocent."
Wren walks in the dark as if it were noon, and whistles very softly so you can follow.
road_cold: Wren produces, from one of her pockets, a flask of something that warms you down to your boots.
road_hot: Wren: "Hot as a warden's temper. Find some shade."

osric+tobiah: Tobiah: "Were you ever at a hanging, Sir Osric?" Osric: "Many." Tobiah: "Me too. From the other side."
Osric watches Tobiah palm a coin, make it vanish, and make it reappear in Osric's own belt-pouch. "Sir," says Tobiah, "you dropped this."
durgin+aelith: Aelith: "I remember when Kharak-Dûl was built." Durgin: "You would." Aelith: "It was ugly then, too."
Durgin writes something in his book, looking at Aelith. Without turning round, she says: "Spell my name properly."
wendeline+grusha: Wendeline and Grusha dig a grave by the road for a dead pedlar nobody else would touch, and neither of them says a word about it afterwards.
Grusha: "Does it get lighter, Sister?" Wendeline: "No. You get stronger."
tobiah+wren: Wren and Tobiah have a whispered argument about the best way into a walled town, which Wren wins.
Tobiah: "Were you ever caught?" Wren: "Never." Tobiah: "Not once?" Wren: "That's what never means, love."
osric+grusha: Osric: "The Rule says a knight must forgive what is truly repented." Grusha: "Does the Rule say what the dead think?" Osric has no answer, and says so.
wendeline+aelith: Aelith: "I have written down every plague in these lands for five hundred years." Wendeline: "I buried them."
durgin+wren: Wren shares her pipe-weed with Durgin, and Durgin shares his book. They laugh about page nine for an hour.
osric+durgin: Durgin: "A knight, eh? We had those. Mostly they died first." Osric: "That is rather the point of us."
tobiah+aelith: Aelith: "I knew your great-great-grandfather. He was also a thief." Tobiah: "Was he any good?" Aelith: "He was hanged." Tobiah: "Once?"
durgin+grusha: Durgin and Grusha compare scars. Grusha wins, and will not say how she got the last one.
osric+wendeline: Osric: "The Order kept the dead in their graves." Wendeline: "I put them there. Between us we have it covered."
aelith+wren: Wren: "How old are you, really?" Aelith: "Older than every road you know." Wren: "Not the sheep-tracks." Aelith, after a pause: "No. Not the sheep-tracks."
tobiah+grusha: Tobiah tries to lift something from Grusha's pack. Grusha, without looking round, catches his wrist, holds it a moment, and lets it go. Tobiah does not try again.
wendeline+tobiah: Wendeline looks at the rope scar on Tobiah's neck. "Who tied that?" "A drunk." "Hm. Bad knot. Lucky for you."

remembrance: Aelith looks about her. "{text}" she says. "That was in {year}. I remember it as if it were last spring."
"I have been here before," Aelith says. "In {year}. {text} It looked much the same. The people were different."
Aelith stops at the edge of {place}. "{text} I wrote it down the same night, in {year}."
"{year}," Aelith says, to nobody in particular. "{text} Nobody here remembers it. I do."
